\chapter{The Core Verbs}
\label{ch:sa-core-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{7}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that someone is, becomes, goes, comes, eats, sees and knows in Sanskrit; I can name each verb by its dhātu rather than by its present form, say which of the three gaṇa patterns builds its stem, and point at the English word that descends from the same root.}

Say \sk{जानाति}, name its root \sk{ज्ञा} and the syllable -\sk{ना}- its class plants inside the word, run back through the chapter's six verbs as root plus class plus ending, separate the one that is a prefixed form of another, and pair \sk{गम्}, \sk{अद्}, \sk{पश्} and \sk{भू} with come, eat, inspect and be.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[asti · bhavati]{\sk{अस्ति} and \sk{भवति} — Sanskrit's two words for \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:SA-C07-asti}



\begin{quote}
Six chapters of words. Now the machinery. A Sanskrit verb is never quoted the way an English one is, and this pair shows why.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{अस्ति} and \sk{भवति}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\sk{अस्ति} & \emph{asti} & he, she, or it \textbf{is} \\
\sk{भवति} & \emph{bhavati} & he, she, or it \textbf{becomes} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both land in English as \textquotedblleft{}is.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Asti} states that something simply \textbf{is} there. \emph{Bhavati} says something \textbf{comes to be} — a state arriving rather than sitting still. Sanskrit never merged the two.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\sk{अ}} is \emph{a}, a short neutral vowel; \textbf{\sk{ति}} is \emph{ti}. Inside \textbf{\sk{अस्ति}} the \emph{s} and \emph{t} stack into one joined shape, \textbf{\sk{स्ति}} — Devanagari fuses a consonant cluster into a single letter. \textbf{\sk{भवति}} needs no fusing: \textbf{\sk{भ}} \emph{bha}, \textbf{\sk{व}} \emph{va}, \textbf{\sk{ति}} \emph{ti}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the dhātu and its gaṇa}]
Sanskrit files a verb under its \textbf{\sk{धातु}} (\emph{dhātu}), its \textbf{root} — the bare syllable a dictionary lists. \emph{Asti} is filed under \textbf{\sk{अस्}} (\emph{as}), \emph{bhavati} under \textbf{\sk{भू}} (\emph{bhū}).

A root is not yet a word. To reach the present it joins one of ten \textbf{\sk{गण}} (\emph{gaṇa}) classes, and the class decides what happens between root and ending. Class 2 adds nothing: \emph{as} + \emph{ti} $\to$ \emph{asti}. Class 1 strengthens the root and adds a vowel: \emph{bhū} $\to$ \emph{bhava} + \emph{ti} $\to$ \emph{bhavati}.

Root, then class, then ending. Every verb in this chapter is built that way.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\sk{अस्}} is PIE *\emph{es-}: English \textbf{is}, Latin \emph{est}, German \emph{ist}, barely worn.

\textbf{\sk{भू}} is PIE *\emph{bheu-}, \textquotedblleft{}to grow, to come to be\textquotedblright{}: English \textbf{be} and \textbf{been}, Latin \emph{futūrus} behind \textbf{future}, Greek \emph{phusis} behind \textbf{physics}.

Now the surprise. English \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} is stitched from \emph{both} — \emph{am, is, are} from *\emph{es-}; \emph{be, been, being} from *\emph{bheu-}. English fused two verbs into one ragged paradigm. Sanskrit left them side by side.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}asti\textquotedblright{} — it is
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bhavati\textquotedblright{} — it becomes
  \item the two roots — \emph{as}, \emph{bhū}
  \item the English halves — \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} from one, \textquotedblleft{}been\textquotedblright{} from the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two roots stand behind \emph{asti} and \emph{bhavati}? (\textbf{\sk{अस्}} \emph{as} and \textbf{\sk{भू}} \emph{bhū}.) What does a \sk{गण} class do? (\textbf{Turns a root into a present stem} — nothing added for \emph{as}, a vowel added for \emph{bhū}.) Which English words descend from each? (\emph{Is} from \emph{as}; \emph{be} and \emph{been} from \emph{bhū}.) Next: a root whose present stem you could never have guessed.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gacchati]{\sk{गच्छति} (gacchati) — \textquotedblleft{}goes,\textquotedblright{} and why dictionaries file it elsewhere}

\label{lesson:SA-C07-gacchati}



\begin{quote}
Root, then class, then ending. Say the two roots from last time. (\emph{As}, \emph{bhū}.) Here the middle step stops being tidy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{गच्छति}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\sk{गच्छति} & \emph{gacchati} & he, she, or it \textbf{goes} \\
\sk{गच्छामि} & \emph{gacchāmi} & \textbf{I} go \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The second form is already yours: Chapter 4 used it to take leave. Same stem, different ending — \textbf{-\sk{ति}} \emph{-ti} for \textquotedblleft{}he, she, it,\textquotedblright{} \textbf{-\sk{ामि}} \emph{-āmi} for \textquotedblleft{}I.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\sk{ग}} is \emph{ga}. \textbf{\sk{ति}} is \emph{ti}, already familiar. Between them sits \textbf{\sk{च्छ}}, a doubled \emph{ch} — one stacked shape for two \emph{ch} sounds in a row, held slightly long: \emph{gach-cha}. Let the middle of the word linger.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the stem that hides its root}]
The root here is \textbf{\sk{गम्}} (\emph{gam}), \textquotedblleft{}to go.\textquotedblright{} The present stem is \textbf{\sk{गच्छ}} (\emph{gaccha}). No rule you have met turns one into the other, and no amount of staring at \emph{gaccha} recovers \emph{gam}.

That is the whole reason Sanskrit hangs its grammar on the root rather than on any spoken form. \emph{Gam} is where the dictionary keeps this verb, where its past and future are built from, and where its relatives — \textbf{\sk{गति}} \emph{gati} \textquotedblleft{}motion,\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\sk{आगम}} \emph{āgama} \textquotedblleft{}arrival\textquotedblright{} — are visibly cousins. Learn roots, not forms.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\sk{गम्}} is PIE *\emph{gwem-}. Its English descendant is \textbf{come} — the same root, turned around: what one language walks away with, another walks toward.

Latin took it as \emph{venīre}, \textquotedblleft{}to come,\textquotedblright{} and English then borrowed it back in a crowd: \textbf{venue}, \textbf{convene}, \textbf{intervene}, \textbf{advent}, \textbf{adventure}. Sanskrit \emph{gacchati} and English \emph{come} are the two ends of one very old word.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gacchati\textquotedblright{} — it goes
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gacchāmi\textquotedblright{} — I go
  \item the root, not the stem — \emph{gam}
  \item the English cousin — \emph{come}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the root of \emph{gacchati}? (\textbf{\sk{गम्}} \emph{gam}.) Could you have predicted the stem from it? (\textbf{No} — which is why the root is what gets learned.) Which ending makes it \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{-\sk{ामि}} \emph{-āmi}.) Which English verb is the same root? (\textbf{Come}.) Next: the same stem, aimed the other way.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āgacchati]{\sk{आगच्छति} (āgacchati) — \textquotedblleft{}comes,\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}goes\textquotedblright{} reversed}

\label{lesson:SA-C07-agacchati}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}it goes.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Gacchati}.) Now add one syllable in front and the direction reverses.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{आगच्छति}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\sk{गच्छति} & \emph{gacchati} & it \textbf{goes} \\
\sk{आगच्छति} & \emph{āgacchati} & it \textbf{comes} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\sk{आ}} (\emph{ā}) means \textquotedblleft{}toward, hither.\textquotedblright{} Stick it on the front and the motion turns back to face you. Sanskrit has no separate word for \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{} at all: coming is going, aimed homeward.

\begin{sounds}
Everything after the first letter is last lesson's word, unchanged. The new piece is \textbf{\sk{आ}}, the long \emph{ā} — the same vowel as \textbf{\sk{अ}} \emph{a} but held roughly twice as long. Length alone carries meaning in Sanskrit, so give it its time: \emph{aa-gach-cha-ti}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the upasarga, Sanskrit's aiming device}]
\textbf{\sk{आ}} is an \textbf{\sk{उपसर्ग}} (\emph{upasarga}), a preverb. Sanskrit has about twenty, and any of them may ride in front of a root to re-aim it:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{prefix} & \textbf{sense} & \textbf{on \sk{गम्}} \\
\midrule
\sk{आ} \emph{ā} & toward & \emph{āgacchati}, comes \\
\sk{सम्} \emph{sam} & together & \emph{saṁgacchati}, goes together \\
\sk{नि} \emph{ni} & down & \emph{nigacchati}, goes down \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A handful of roots plus a handful of prefixes covers an enormous amount of vocabulary. You have met the trick already without being told: \textbf{\sk{संस्कृत}} (\emph{saṁskṛta}, \textquotedblleft{}Sanskrit\textquotedblright{}) is \emph{sam} \textquotedblleft{}together\textquotedblright{} on the root \sk{कृ} \emph{kṛ} \textquotedblleft{}make\textquotedblright{} — put-together, and so perfected.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin aims \emph{venīre} \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{} with the same kind of prefix: \emph{ad-} \textquotedblleft{}toward\textquotedblright{} gives \textbf{advent}, \emph{con-} \textquotedblleft{}with\textquotedblright{} gives \textbf{convene}, \emph{inter-} \textquotedblleft{}between\textquotedblright{} gives \textbf{intervene}. English does it natively too — \emph{come} becomes \textbf{become}, \textbf{overcome}, \textbf{income}.

Sanskrit simply runs the system harder and more openly, with the seams left visible.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gacchati … āgacchati\textquotedblright{} — goes, comes
  \item the prefix and its sense — \emph{ā}, toward
  \item one more prefix on the same root — \emph{sam}, together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Sanskrit say \textquotedblleft{}comes\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\sk{आगच्छति}} — \emph{ā} \textquotedblleft{}toward\textquotedblright{} on \textquotedblleft{}goes.\textquotedblright{}) What is such a prefix called? (An \textbf{\sk{उपसर्ग}}, \emph{upasarga}.) Which Sanskrit word you already knew is built the same way? (\textbf{\sk{संस्कृत}} — \emph{sam} plus \emph{kṛ}.) Next: a verb whose everyday form is not the one related to English.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[khādati]{\sk{खादति} (khādati) — \textquotedblleft{}eats,\textquotedblright{} and the cousin it is not}

\label{lesson:SA-C07-khadati}



\begin{quote}
Name the three steps that build a Sanskrit present. (\textbf{Root, class, ending}.) This verb is the tidiest one yet — and hides a warning.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{खादति}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\sk{खादति} & \emph{khādati} & he, she, or it \textbf{eats} \\
\sk{खाद्य} & \emph{khādya} & \textbf{edible}, food \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The root is \textbf{\sk{खाद्}} (\emph{khād}), and it belongs to the same class 1 as \emph{bhū}, so the build is plain: \emph{khād} + \emph{a} + \emph{ti} $\to$ \emph{khādati}. No stacked letters, no surprises, nothing hidden.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\sk{खा}} is \emph{khā}: a \emph{k} with a puff of breath after it, then the long \emph{ā} you met last lesson. Sanskrit treats that puff as a separate letter, not an accent — \textbf{\sk{क}} \emph{ka} and \textbf{\sk{ख}} \emph{kha} are two different letters that change meaning. \textbf{\sk{द}} is \emph{da}, \textbf{\sk{ति}} is \emph{ti}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the everyday word and the related word}]
English \textbf{eat}, Latin \emph{edere} (behind \textbf{edible}), and German \emph{essen} all descend from PIE *\emph{ed-}. Sanskrit inherited it too, as the root \textbf{\sk{अद्}} (\emph{ad}), class 2 — endings straight onto the root, like \emph{asti}: \emph{ad} + \emph{ti} $\to$ \textbf{\sk{अत्ति}} (\emph{atti}), \textquotedblleft{}eats.\textquotedblright{}

But \emph{atti} is not the ordinary word. Classical Sanskrit eats with \textbf{\sk{खाद्}}, a root with no clear European relative at all.

So the family word and the everyday word part company here. Cognates tell you where a language came from; they do not promise to tell you what it says at dinner. Keep the two questions separate.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
The pattern repeats across the family. English has native \textbf{eat} beside borrowed \textbf{consume} and \textbf{devour}; Sanskrit has inherited \textbf{\sk{अद्}} beside ordinary \textbf{\sk{खाद्}}.

A language keeps its old word somewhere — in a proverb, a compound, a sacred text — while daily speech moves on to another. \emph{Khādya}, \textquotedblleft{}edible,\textquotedblright{} is the word you will actually meet on a menu.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}khādati\textquotedblright{} — it eats
  \item the root and its class build — \emph{khād} … \emph{a} … \emph{ti}
  \item the cousin of English \emph{eat} — \emph{ad}, \emph{atti}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the ordinary Sanskrit verb for eating? (\textbf{\sk{खादति}}, \emph{khādati}, root \textbf{\sk{खाद्}}.) Which Sanskrit root is the actual cousin of English \emph{eat}? (\textbf{\sk{अद्}} \emph{ad}, giving \emph{atti}.) Which class does \emph{ad} belong to, and how do you know? (\textbf{Class 2} — the ending goes straight onto the root, as in \emph{asti}.) Next: a verb built out of two different roots.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[paśyati]{\sk{पश्यति} (paśyati) — \textquotedblleft{}sees,\textquotedblright{} a verb with two roots}

\label{lesson:SA-C07-pashyati}



\begin{quote}
So far one root has built each verb. Here two roots share the work, and you have already met the quieter one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{पश्यति}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\sk{पश्यति} & \emph{paśyati} & he, she, or it \textbf{sees} \\
\sk{दर्शन} & \emph{darśana} & a \textbf{beholding}, a viewing \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The present tense comes from the root \textbf{\sk{पश्}} (\emph{paś}). Every other tense of this verb comes from a different root, \textbf{\sk{दृश्}} (\emph{dṛś}) — and \emph{dṛś} is where \textbf{\sk{दर्शन}} was built, the word inside Chapter 4's farewell \textbf{\sk{पुनर्दर्शनाय}}, \textquotedblleft{}until a seeing again.\textquotedblright{}

Two roots, one verb, divided by tense. English does the same with \emph{go} and \emph{went}, which were never the same verb either.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\sk{प}} is \emph{pa}. Then \textbf{\sk{श्य}}, a stack of two letters: \textbf{\sk{श}} \emph{śa}, a \emph{sh} made with the tongue high and forward, plus \textbf{\sk{य}} \emph{ya}. Say them glued: \emph{pash-ya-ti}. Sanskrit has three different \emph{s} letters, and this is the one that leans toward \emph{sh}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\sk{पश्}} descends from PIE *\emph{spek-}, \textquotedblleft{}to observe closely.\textquotedblright{} The \emph{s} and the \emph{p} swapped places on the way into Indo-Iranian, which is why the Sanskrit form begins \emph{paś-} rather than \emph{spaś-}.

Latin kept it straight as \emph{specere}, and English is full of the results: \textbf{spectacle}, \textbf{inspect}, \textbf{respect}, \textbf{species}, \textbf{suspect}, \textbf{spy}.

Greek swapped the letters too, in its own direction, giving \emph{skop-}: \textbf{telescope}, \textbf{microscope}, \textbf{skeptic}, \textbf{bishop} (from \emph{episkopos}, an overseer).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}paśyati\textquotedblright{} — it sees
  \item the two roots — \emph{paś} for the present, \emph{dṛś} for the rest
  \item the Chapter 4 word from the other root — \emph{darśana}
  \item the English descendants — \emph{inspect}, \emph{species}, \emph{telescope}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which root gives the present \emph{paśyati}? (\textbf{\sk{पश्}} \emph{paś}.) Which root supplies the rest of the verb? (\textbf{\sk{दृश्}} \emph{dṛś} — the one behind \emph{darśana}.) What PIE root is \emph{paś} from? (*\emph{Spek-}.) Name two English words from it. (\textbf{Inspect}, \textbf{species}, \textbf{telescope} — any two.) Next: the verb that means \textquotedblleft{}know,\textquotedblright{} and the class that plants a syllable in the middle.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jānāti]{\sk{जानाति} (jānāti) — \textquotedblleft{}knows,\textquotedblright{} and English \emph{know} is the same word}

\label{lesson:SA-C07-janati}



\begin{quote}
Two ways a root has become a stem so far: nothing added, or a vowel added. Here is the third, and it is the boldest.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{जानाति}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\sk{जानाति} & \emph{jānāti} & he, she, or it \textbf{knows} \\
\sk{ज्ञान} & \emph{jñāna} & \textbf{knowledge} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The root is \textbf{\sk{ज्ञा}} (\emph{jñā}). Its class, the ninth, does not add a vowel at the end — it plants a whole syllable \textbf{-\sk{ना}-} (\emph{-nā-}) between root and ending: \emph{jā} + \emph{nā} + \emph{ti} $\to$ \emph{jānāti}. The marker sits inside the word.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\sk{जा}} is \emph{jā}; \textbf{\sk{ना}} \emph{nā} and \textbf{\sk{ति}} \emph{ti} close it. The root's own spelling \textbf{\sk{ज्ञ}} is a famous stacked letter, \emph{j} over \emph{ñ}, said \emph{gya} across much of India today and \emph{jña} in the classical description. Pick one and stay with it.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\sk{ज्ञा}} is PIE *\emph{gno-}. English \textbf{know} is that root undisguised, and so are \textbf{can} and \textbf{cunning}, which began as \textquotedblleft{}know how.\textquotedblright{}

Latin took it as \emph{noscere}: \textbf{notice}, \textbf{notion}, \textbf{cognition}, \textbf{ignore} (\textquotedblleft{}not-know\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{noble} (\textquotedblleft{}well-known\textquotedblright{}). Greek took it as \emph{gnōsis}: \textbf{diagnosis}, \textbf{prognosis}, \textbf{agnostic}.

One root, a whole shelf of English vocabulary, and Sanskrit \textbf{\sk{ज्ञान}} \emph{jñāna} sitting at the other end of it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: six verbs, three ways to build a stem}]
\emph{Asti}, \emph{bhavati}, \emph{gacchati}, \emph{āgacchati}, \emph{khādati}, \emph{paśyati}, \emph{jānāti}. Every one is a root plus a class plus an ending, and the class was the only thing that varied: nothing inserted (\emph{as-ti}), a vowel appended (\emph{bhava-ti}, \emph{khāda-ti}), or a syllable planted inside (\emph{jā-nā-ti}). Prefix one and you aim it: \emph{ā-gacchati}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}jānāti\textquotedblright{} — it knows
  \item the root and its planted syllable — \emph{jñā} … \emph{nā}
  \item the English twin — \emph{know}
  \item three roots and their English kin — \emph{gam}/come, \emph{ad}/eat, \emph{paś}/inspect
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the root of \emph{jānāti}, and what does its class insert? (\textbf{\sk{ज्ञा}} \emph{jñā}; the syllable \textbf{-\sk{ना}-}.) Give the six verbs of this chapter. (\emph{Asti}, \emph{gacchati}, \emph{āgacchati}, \emph{khādati}, \emph{paśyati}, \emph{jānāti}.) Which two are one root plus a prefix? (\textbf{\sk{गच्छति}} and \textbf{\sk{आगच्छति}}.) Which Sanskrit root is English \emph{know}? (\textbf{\sk{ज्ञा}}.) And which English words carry \emph{gam}, \emph{ad}, \emph{paś}, and \emph{bhū}? (\emph{Come}, \emph{eat}, \emph{inspect}, \emph{be} — four roots you now own in two languages.)
\end{tcolorbox}
